summary: Give the Debt avalanche calculator the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1, the interest rate #2 and the payment #1 and it returns total debt. It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Debt avalanche calculator work?
sections.html:
The Debt avalanche calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total debt in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 6), the interest rate boxes (numbered 1 to 6) and the payment boxes (numbered 1 to 6).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Debt avalanche calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total debt=(balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, how many debts do you have?)
Debt cur apr=(balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, how many debts do you have?, interest rate #1, interest rate #2, interest rate #3, interest rate #4, interest rate #5, interest rate #6, payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6)
Debt apr=((balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, how many debts do you have?, interest rate #1, interest rate #2, interest rate #3, interest rate #4, interest rate #5, interest rate #6, payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6))
Pmt month=((balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, how many debts do you have?, interest rate #1, interest rate #2, interest rate #3, interest rate #4, interest rate #5, interest rate #6, payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6))
Debt cur period=((balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, how many debts do you have?, interest rate #1, interest rate #2, interest rate #3, interest rate #4, interest rate #5, interest rate #6, payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6))
Debt period=((balance #1, balance #2, balance #3, balance #4, balance #5, balance #6, how many debts do you have?, interest rate #1, interest rate #2, interest rate #3, interest rate #4, interest rate #5, interest rate #6, payment #1, payment #2, payment #3, payment #4, payment #5, payment #6))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Debt avalanche calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1 and the interest rate #2 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Debt avalanche calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total debt, derived from the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1 and the interest rate #2. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Debt avalanche calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the balance boxes (numbered 1 to 3), the interest rate #1, the interest rate #2 and the payment #1, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter balance #1 in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Balance #1 opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Debt avalanche calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
